title: Tangkhul Primer and Catechism
subject: Language Primer and Education
notes: Earliest printed document reducing the Tangkhul language to the Roman script, compiled at Ukhrul in 1897.

front_matter.preface: Tangkhul Primer and Catechism (Ukhrul, 1897) compiled by Rev. William Pettigrew. This historic work represents the very first printed book in the Tangkhul Naga language using the Roman alphabet, laying the foundations of modern Tangkhul literacy.

table_of_contents.title: The Verbal System: Tenses, Moods & Causatives

chapters.title: Orthography, Vowels & Consonantal Phonetics
chapters.summary: The Roman alphabet system adapted for Tangkhul, macron markings, and glottal accents.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul Naga tuihi Roman script eina kapi shiyan khare. Vowels ā, ē, ī, ō, ū hi khangashan kachung lei. Kakhalat kashak: 'a' kachihi khangarom tui, 'ā' kachihi khamashung kashak. Glottal stop (') hi tuikashak ngachaili shiyan kashakna.
chapters.english_translation: The Tangkhul language was reduced to writing using the Roman alphabet. Vowel quantity is distinguished with macrons. Short vowels contrast with long vowels. The glottal stop (') marks vital tonal and grammatical separations in the Ukhrul dialect.
grammar_points: Vowel length alters word meaning: e.g. ka vs kā, sha vs shā.
Syllabic structure is CV, CVC, or CCV.
comprehension_questions: Why was the macron introduced in Pettigrew's 1918 orthography?
Give examples of syllable-final consonants in Tangkhul.

chapters.title: Noun Morphology, Gender & Case Suffixes
chapters.tangkhul_text: Tuiwon kasak shiyan: Agentive -na, Dative -li, Possessive -wui, Instrumental -eina. Shimwui ava (master of house), mayarnaona ot sai (the boy does work). Gender: mayār (masculine), va (feminine).
chapters.english_translation: Declension of nouns follows agglutinative postpositions. Agentive marker -na identifies the transitive subject. Genitive -wui indicates relationship, origin, and possession. Grammatical gender does not exist; biological sex is indicated by suffixal markers.
grammar_points: Postposition -eina marks both instrument ('with') and source ('from').
Plural marker -bing follows the noun base and precedes case particles.
comprehension_questions: Distinguish between nominative and agentive uses in Tangkhul.

chapters.title: Adjectives, Degrees of Comparison & Numerals
chapters.summary: Prefix ka-, superlative pamei, and complete numeral tables from 1 to 100.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Kaphā (good), kaphāmei (better), pamei (best). Kasau (tall), kazing (deep). Numbers: akha (1), khani (2), kathum (3), mati (4), phangā (5), tharuk (6), shini (7), chishat (8), chiko (9), thakharā (10), magā khani (20), shā akha (100).
chapters.english_translation: Adjectives usually follow their governing nouns: e.g. mi kaphā (a good man). Comparative suffix -mei; superlative pamei. Decimals: 10 is thakharā or magā, 20 is magā khani, 100 is shā akha.
grammar_points: Attributive adjectives follow nouns; predicate adjectives stand sentence-finally.
Numerals follow the noun: mi kathum = three men.
comprehension_questions: Where does an attributive adjective place relative to its noun?

chapters.title: Pronouns: Personal, Demonstrative & Interrogative
chapters.summary: Pronoun declensions, inclusive vs exclusive first person, and demonstratives hi/chi.
chapters.tangkhul_text: I (I), na (thou), a (he/she/it). Ithum (we), nathum (you all), athum (they). Hi (this), chi (that). Khi (what), khipa (who), khishiwui (whose), kachi (which). Iwui shimli unglo (come to my house).
chapters.english_translation: Personal pronouns take the same case suffixes as nouns: ina, ili, iwui. Demonstrative pronouns hi (proximal: this) and chi (distal: that). Interrogative pronouns: khipa (who), khi (what), kachi (which).
grammar_points: Interrogatives remain in situ and do not trigger inversion.
Possessive pronouns precede or follow nouns depending on emphasis.
comprehension_questions: Form the complete case declension of pronoun 'i' (I).
What is the difference between 'hi' and 'chi'?

chapters.title: The Verbal System: Tenses, Moods & Causatives
chapters.summary: Conjugations, aspectual particles, auxiliaries lei and sa, and passive/causative morphemes.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Present: i sai (I make/do). Past: i sada / i saser (I made/did). Future: i sara (I will make/do). Subjunctive: a va-akha (if he goes). Causative: i ali sa-sak-ei (I cause him to do). Auxiliary: lei (to exist, to have), sa (to do, to be).
chapters.english_translation: Verbal morphology is rich and precise: tense inflections, conditional suffixes (-akha), and causative markers (-sak). Existential auxiliary 'lei' expresses location and possession.

vocabulary.meaning: to exist, to dwell, to be present

grammar_points: Conditional clauses end in verb root + -akha ('if').
Existential 'lei' takes possessor in dative-locative (-li): ili lairik lei = I have a book.
comprehension_questions: How is possession expressed using the verb 'lei'?
Give the conditional form of 'kathei' (to see).

chapters.title: Conversational Phrases & Everyday Village Life
chapters.summary: Phrases for greeting, agricultural work, village council affairs, and family relations.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khangachan: 'Na katha lei?' -- 'I phaida lei.' 'Nawui ming khi hoyno?' -- 'Iwui ming Somi hoyei.' 'Lui kasak tharan zingshorli kaphung ngashitda ot kasa phamei.' 'Iram Ukhrulli won kapha wonri.'
chapters.english_translation: Conversational exchanges: 'How are you?' -- 'I am well.' 'What is your name?' -- 'My name is Somi.' 'During terrace cultivation, working together on the eastern hills is best.' 'In our Ukhrul homeland, lovely blooms flourish.'
comprehension_questions: Translate into Tangkhul: 'What is your father's name?'
How do Tangkhuls greet one another in daily conversation?

excerpts.translation_en: Selected alphabetical entries from Pettigrew's 1918 Lexicon, providing part of speech, etymological derivations, and definitions in English.
